extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, history of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria for constructing and applying a Baconian inductive method in natural and other sciences: how to collect, order, and interpret facts, when to generalize, and what ends scientific inquiry should serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of simple natures (simplices naturae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover the ultimate elements ('simple natures') out of which complex natural effects are compounded; these are analogous to letters of the alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse each instance (instantia) into its simple natures and then, by rejecting one after another (method of Exclusion), ascertain the Form or Cause of the phenomenon. This analysis is the foundation for certain knowledge and for applying the method of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exclusion applied to well-examined instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Use attentive consideration of each instance to analyse it into constituent simple natures and exclude candidates to identify causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method requires patient diligence and ordinary acuteness; examine instantiae carefully and apply exclusion sequentially. The passage compares this to analysing letters in words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer real, non-fictitious experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek genuine ('non-fictitious') experiments and observations rather than contrived or merely hypothetical ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from actual experiments and the 'creation' example: begin with what nature produces (like light) rather than inventing fictive cases; avoid asking for fictitious experiments at the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature speculative subtilty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indulge in speculative subtilities (over-subtle dialectical refinements) before establishing axioms from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtlety of disputation applied before axioms are found is 'seram et praeposteram' (untimely and backward). Subtlety's proper time is in pondering prepared experience and in constructing axioms from that experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish fundamentals even if seemingly useless
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that simple elements and seeds of things may be of little apparent use by themselves but are necessary as the materia prima for composition and further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters (literarum elementa) alone signify nothing but are necessary for composing speech; similarly, simple natures give access to the interior of works and to axioms—thus they must be sought despite immediate lack of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base discovery on nature, not antiquity or authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek inventions and discoveries from the light of nature rather than by appealing to ancient authorities or claiming antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject reliance on comment and imposture and do not concern whether a thing was known to the ancients; invention should be sought from nature's light, not repeated from antiquity's darkness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and utility as the proper ends of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief objects of this kind of inquiry are Truth and Usefulness (Veritas et utilitas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should be valued as tokens of truth and usefulness; knowledge of facts (res) leads to both truth and rules for practice. The Baconian method aims at both contemplative truth and practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare ordered histories and tables before interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile and order history (historia) and tables (tabulae) of observations for the subject before proceeding to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For any subject—natural or mental—prepare collected facts and orderly tables (e.g., of anger, fear, memory, etc.) as a prerequisite to correct interpretation and the establishment of axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed to generalisation by middle steps; suspend premature judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pronounce final principles or axioms until intermediate stages of inquiry have been reached through progressive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain suspension of judgment until the proper middle grades to general-level principles are obtained through the method; avoid leaping at once to universal principles which can lead to acatalepsia (unresolvable skepticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the inductive method across sciences with adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of interpretation (induction) pertains to all sciences—natural, logical, ethical, political—and can be adapted to their different subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although primarily aimed at natural philosophy, the method extends to moral and mental sciences; interpretation must be fitted to the quality and condition of the objects investigated, and different combinations of methods apply to, e.g., mechanics, chemistry, physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the senses as servants and govern the intellect; avoid claiming total knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not derogate the senses but minister to them; govern rather than despise the intellect; better to know how much is needed and yet not claim complete knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate a posture of 'Eucatalepsia' (faith in attainable knowledge) rather than absolute skepticism; be modest about the extent of knowledge while using senses and intellect cooperatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect and anatomise the world to found true exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish true exemplars of the world in the human intellect by careful dissection and anatomy of the facts of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A detailed, patient dissection of the world's facts is necessary to produce correct exemplars; fanciful or inept 'models' and 'mimicries' constructed by human imagination should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and incorporate useful existing science
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not aim to demolish the established sciences and arts; accept their use, cultivation, and honors where they are valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing learned arts and disputations may be used for instruction and civil advantage; the new method warns only that popular comprehension may require demonstration by effects and works rather than mere words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce results and works to persuade general audience
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure acceptance by the public or the vulgar understanding, scientific claims must be backed by effects and works rather than by abstract argument alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that the general public is convinced chiefly by practical demonstrations and useful outcomes; publication alone of phil. treatises (e.g., De Progressu Scientiarum) evidences goodwill, but works/effects are required to bring ideas to the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value transformative inventions as primary markers of scientific importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the greatness of discoveries by their effect on human affairs—e.g., printing, gunpowder, and navigation changed literature, war, and navigation respectively, altering the state of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating inventions or sciences, consider how they alter the condition, administration, or capability of human life across time and place; inventions that yield lasting, wide benefits deserve high honor.
